SOLO 401(K) CONTRIBUTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How much can you put in your Solo 401(k) in 2026?

For a sole proprietor or single-member LLC: an employee elective deferral of up to $24,500 (more with a catch-up), plus an employer profit-sharing contribution of 20% of your net self-employment earnings, combined up to $72,000 (more with a catch-up) for 2026.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Your business and age

Net profit is your Schedule C net profit (or a single-member LLC's equivalent), before this retirement contribution — not gross revenue.

2. Optional adjustments

The elective-deferral limit is shared across every 401(k) you contribute to — including a separate W-2 employer's plan — not per plan. Enter what you have already deferred elsewhere this year if any.

Enter your net profit and age, then click Calculate.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Sole proprietor / single-member LLC only. This applies the net-self-employment-earnings formula for a Schedule C filer with no W-2 wages from the business. An S-corp or partnership uses a different formula (W-2 wages or a K-1 allocation) and this tool does not compute it.
  • Not a Schedule SE substitute. This ignores the additional 0.9% Medicare surtax above $200,000/$250,000 and does not account for multiple businesses or controlled-group rules.
  • Roth, after-tax, and mega-backdoor splits are not modelled. This computes the total contribution room, not how to split it between traditional, Roth, or (if your plan allows it) after-tax employee contributions.
  • Point-in-time 2026 figures. These limits are re-indexed annually; confirm the current year's figures before relying on this in a later year.

Common questions

What is the 2026 Solo 401(k) contribution limit?

The employee elective deferral is $24,500 for 2026 ($32,500 with the age-50 catch-up, or $35,750 with the SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for ages 60-63). Added to a 20% employer profit-sharing contribution from net self-employment earnings, the combined total is capped at $72,000, or $80,000 with the standard catch-up, or $83,250 with the enhanced 60-63 catch-up.

How is the employer profit-sharing contribution calculated for a sole proprietor?

Net profit minus half of self-employment tax gives net earnings from self-employment. A plan stating a 25% employer contribution rate converts to an effective 20% rate applied to that net-earnings figure for a sole proprietor or single-member LLC, because the contribution is itself computed on earnings net of the contribution.

Does the elective-deferral limit apply separately to a Solo 401(k) and a W-2 job's 401(k)?

No. The elective-deferral limit applies per person across every 401(k) plan combined, including a separate employer's plan. Deferrals already made at a W-2 job reduce the room left for the Solo 401(k) dollar for dollar.

What is the enhanced catch-up for ages 60-63?

SECURE 2.0 gives ages 60, 61, 62, and 63 an $11,250 catch-up for 2026 instead of the standard $8,000 catch-up — it replaces rather than stacks with the standard amount, and the plan document must specifically allow it.

Is this tax advice?

No. This tool applies published 2026 IRS figures to the numbers you enter, scoped to a sole proprietor or single-member LLC with no W-2 wages from the business. It does not replace IRS Publication 560 or a qualified tax professional, and an S-corp or partnership uses a different formula entirely.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own plan's terms before contributing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (limit_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Prefer a simpler plan? The SEP-IRA contribution calculator shows the employer-only limit for the same earnings.

Not sure a Solo 401(k) beats a SEP-IRA for you? The SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) calculator compares the two at your profit and shows what the gap is worth in tax.

Wondering why not just work the IRS worksheet yourself? See this calculator vs. IRS Publication 560 by hand.

High income and over 40? A cash balance plan calculator estimates a much larger deductible contribution alongside a 401(k).

Maximizing an after-tax 401(k) at a W-2 job instead? The mega backdoor Roth calculator is the one for that — a different plan type and a different eligibility mechanism entirely.

Deducting a business car as a self-employed filer? The mileage deduction method calculator compares the 2026 standard mileage rate with actual vehicle expenses.

Setting up a plan for your staff? The retirement plan startup credit calculator shows how much of the setup and employer contributions the IRS credit covers.

Run a business with employees? The 401(k) plan fee calculator adds up a plan's all-in cost and compares it with an editable size benchmark.

Missed the Form 5500 deadline for a plan like this? The Form 5500 late filing calculator shows the due date and the DFVC cost against IRS and DOL penalty exposure.

Deducting a home office too? The home office deduction calculator compares the simplified and regular methods.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-irs-publication-560-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Solo 401(k) Contribution Calculator

This calculator vs. working IRS Publication 560 by hand

This names no specific firm or product. It compares a free browser tool against the generic method most self-employed people use: searching "solo 401k contribution limit 2026", landing on the IRS worksheet in Publication 560, and working out the employer contribution with a calculator or spreadsheet of their own.

QuestionWorking Publication 560 by handThis calculator
Employer contribution rate Publication 560 describes a plan rate of up to 25% of compensation, but for a sole proprietor the rate is effectively 20% of earnings net of the deduction, because the contribution is itself deducted; reading "25%" and applying it to net profit is a common slip Applies 20% to net earnings from self-employment, so the circular calculation is already resolved
Self-employment tax adjustment You compute SE tax on 92.35% of net profit (12.4% Social Security up to the $184,500 2026 wage base, 2.9% Medicare uncapped), halve it, and subtract it before applying the rate Does each step in order and shows the intermediate figures
Elective deferral and catch-up You look up the $24,500 limit and work out which catch-up applies at your age: $8,000 at 50-59 and 64+, or the SECURE 2.0 $11,250 for ages 60-63 in place of, not on top of, the standard one Takes your age and picks the right catch-up automatically
Combined overall limit Employee deferral plus employer contribution cannot exceed the Section 415(c) limit ($72,000, $80,000 or $83,250 by catch-up), and earnings above the $360,000 compensation limit are ignored Caps the total at the overall limit and states which cap applied
Deferrals at a W-2 job Easy to forget that the deferral limit is shared across plans; you subtract what the other plan already took yourself Has an input for deferrals already made elsewhere and reduces your room
Authority behind the answer IRS Publication 560 and IRS.gov are the primary source A calculation aid, not a determination. Uses the same published figures; does not verify your plan document, which must allow the enhanced catch-up
Where your numbers go while you work this out Depends on your spreadsheet or note app, which may sync to a cloud account Held in page memory only. Nothing is uploaded and there is no server component
Opening or funding the plan Your plan provider handles that Never contacts a provider and contributes nothing; you remain responsible for the actual contribution

Neither approach verifies your plan document or files anything for you. Both are only as good as the figures you bring, and both should be checked against IRS.gov before you contribute.

Common questions

Why not just work through IRS Publication 560 myself?

Publication 560 is the primary source and this tool does not replace it. The friction is the arithmetic: you take net profit, work out self-employment tax on 92.35% of it, halve that tax, subtract it, and then apply 20% (the effective rate for a stated 25% plan rate) to what is left. Skipping the self-employment-tax step and applying 20% or 25% to net profit overstates the employer contribution, and an overstated contribution is the mistake that can lead to an excess-contribution excise tax.

Does this replace a tax professional?

No. It applies published 2026 IRS figures to the numbers you enter, for a sole proprietor or single-member LLC filing Schedule C with no W-2 wages from the business. It is not tax advice. An S-corp or partnership uses a different formula, and an unusual situation is a question for a qualified tax professional, not a web page.

What if I also have a 401(k) at a W-2 job?

The employee elective-deferral limit is shared across every plan you participate in, not doubled. Enter what you have already deferred at the other job and the calculator reduces your Solo 401(k) deferral room accordingly.

No warranty. This page is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. IRS limits change every year — verify the current figures on IRS.gov before you contribute.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice.

Use the Solo 401(k) Contribution Calculator to work out your own limit.
